hook.headline: One transaction can see two committed realities
hook.hook: Under PostgreSQL Read Committed, each statement gets its own snapshot, so later queries can observe newly committed concurrent changes.
hook.visualCaption: A transaction boundary does not imply one fixed read snapshot at Read Committed.
hook.microExample: SELECT #1 → concurrent COMMIT → SELECT #2 may see newer data

mentalModel.title: Snapshots are statement-scoped
mentalModel.coreIdea: PostgreSQL Read Committed gives each ordinary SELECT a snapshot taken when that query begins. A later SELECT in the same transaction gets a new snapshot, so commits completed in between can become visible without exposing uncommitted data.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Successive reads can differ because visibility is recalculated from a new committed snapshot.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: statement → snapshot → visible commits → next statement

code.title: Two reads, two snapshots
code.intro: The transaction stays open, but Read Committed does not freeze one snapshot for every query.
code.highlightReason: The second SELECT receives a new statement snapshot, so it can observe a concurrent change committed after the first SELECT began.
code.takeaway: Transaction scope and snapshot scope are different concepts at PostgreSQL Read Committed.
code.professionalNote: The second result can differ; it is not a dirty read because the observed change was committed.

production.title: When this surprises services
production.scenario: A service reads an order, performs more work, then reads it again in the same transaction and sees a newer status committed by another request.
problems: Assuming BEGIN freezes one database view.
Making multi-step decisions from reads that may observe different committed states.
production.professionalApproach: If a workflow requires a stable view across multiple queries, choose an isolation strategy that provides it, such as PostgreSQL Repeatable Read, and account for concurrent-write conflicts where relevant.
production.debugClue: Two SELECTs in one transaction return different committed values without any rollback or dirty read.

interview.question: A PostgreSQL transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values. No dirty read occurred. How is that possible?
interview.answer: At PostgreSQL Read Committed, each SELECT uses a snapshot taken when that statement begins. If another transaction commits an update between the two reads, the second SELECT can see it. That is still Read Committed, not a dirty read. For a stable transaction-wide snapshot, consider Repeatable Read and its concurrency implications.
